network.overall_strategy: This connected network contains ten selected pathways: seven variants of sulfur-assisted aromatic Strecker chemistry, two mineral-dependent reductive-amination pathways, and one experimentally observed discharge-process pathway. These are distinct graph traversals, not ten independently demonstrated syntheses from simple feedstocks. Phenylalanine is represented without stereochemical preference; the expected product is racemic. The principal aromatic source module is explicitly unresolved: energetic hydrocarbon chemistry supports phenylacetylene formation, but the methane-only source reaction is a speculative, lumped material balance rather than an established elementary sequence. Phenylpyruvate is an explicitly supplied complex precursor for the mineral pathways; its autonomous formation from simple geochemical carbon is not claimed. Numerical operating windows are proposed environmental test conditions unless identified as reported experimental conditions. Sulfur-intermediate assignments, environmental hydrolysis rates, cyanide delivery efficiencies, and oxidized mineral products retain stated uncertainties. All modules occupy distinct surface or cooled geothermal compartments under anoxia; no transfer through destructive high-temperature vent interiors is required. Reaction sequences are topological lists that include prerequisite branches, which may operate separately before their products meet. Stoichiometric coefficients appear in mechanism text, never as repeated molecule IDs. Neutral parent formulas represent rapidly interconverting acid-base forms, except where explicit ionic species are needed for iron-cyanide bookkeeping. Terminal coproducts use the permitted intermediate role because the schema lacks a coproduct category.

reactions.name: Discharge generation of atmospheric hydrogen cyanide

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K bulk gas and collector; nonthermal discharge channel
conditions.other: Anoxic, locally reduced methane-ammonia gas above a water collector. Proposed collection interval: 1-24 h with repeated discharges; this is a test envelope, not a reported source-paper duration. HCN must dissolve into nearby water before atmospheric photolysis or escape. Electrical excitation is not represented as an equilibrium gas temperature.

reactions.mechanism: Lumped selected-product balance: CH4 + NH3 -> HCN + 3 H2. Electron-impact fragmentation and radical recombination generate HCN among many other products; this is not a single elementary reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Discharge-generated HCN supplies the cyanide required by the experimentally supported aromatic Strecker sequence (Friedmann and Miller, 1969). Reduced atmospheric mixtures support much greater amino-acid production than insufficiently reduced mixtures (Schlesinger and Miller, 1983). The balance does not imply quantitative selectivity. Collection and concentration are unresolved environmental requirements, and no globally methane-rich atmosphere is assumed.

reactions.name: Unresolved energetic hydrocarbon source of phenylacetylene

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K cooled bulk gas; transient nonthermal discharge
conditions.other: Locally methane-rich volcanic or impact-plume gas, electrical excitation, and immediate capture by condensing water or organic-rich films. Proposed collection interval: 1-24 h. The supplied research provides no methane-specific phenylacetylene production rate, discharge dose, or collection efficiency; none is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Formal selected-product balance: 8 CH4 -> C8H6 + 13 H2. The node lumps fragmentation, carbon-carbon bond formation, ring assembly, and dehydrogenation. Its internal intermediate sequence is unresolved.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE METHANE-SPECIFIC SOURCE MODULE. Friedmann and Miller (1969) supports phenylacetylene production through energetic hydrocarbon chemistry, but does not, in the supplied account, establish this methane-only sequence or its environmental productivity. This node exposes the aromatic-carbon supply gap rather than inventing an acetylene photochemical mechanism. It is necessary only to display a possible simple-carbon entry into the explicit Strecker branch. No end-to-end yield can be assigned until phenylacetylene flux and capture are measured.

reactions.name: Productive ionic sulfide addition to phenylacetylene

conditions.other: Anoxic, shaded sulfide-containing pool; proposed pH 8-9 and residence time 1-24 h. Phenylacetylene is supplied as dissolved material or dispersed organic films. These numerical bounds are environmental hypotheses, not reported Friedmann-Miller conditions. Cyanide and ammonia are introduced only downstream.

reactions.mechanism: Net balance: C8H6 + H2S -> C8H8S. Productive terminal-carbon attack by HS- followed by protonation gives PhCH=CH-SH, represented by mol_008. H2S denotes the total sulfide acid-base pool in the neutral-parent balance.
reactions.reasoning: Friedmann and Miller (1969) supports an ionic sulfur-addition contribution to aldehyde formation. The explicitly drawn anti-Markovnikov thioenol is a mechanistic representation of the productive branch, not a claim that it was isolated or formed selectively under the proposed conditions. Opposite regiochemistry would lead toward an acetophenone-type skeleton, not phenylalanine. Productive regioselectivity and competition with sulfur-containing oligomers remain unquantified.

reactions.name: Productive photoinitiated radical sulfide addition to phenylacetylene

conditions.other: Anoxic sulfide-rich films, proposed pH 6-8. A laboratory screening window would use 254 nm irradiation at 0.1-1 W/m2 for 1-10 h, corresponding to 0.36-36 kJ/m2. These are proposed screening doses, not published yields or reconstructed early-Earth exposures. Withdraw products into shaded water; exclude aldehyde and amino-acid products from this irradiation stage.

reactions.mechanism: Net balance: C8H6 + H2S -> C8H8S. Photogenerated sulfur-centered radicals add to the terminal alkyne carbon; hydrogen-atom transfer completes the productive PhCH=CH-SH branch.
reactions.reasoning: Friedmann and Miller (1969) supports a radical sulfur-addition channel in addition to the ionic channel. The exact useful photon dose, radical-chain efficiency, and product distribution are not established by the supplied report. This pathway is therefore not ranked above rxn_003. The proposed irradiation experiment must establish productive selectivity rather than merely disappearance of phenylacetylene.

reactions.name: Thioenol-thioaldehyde tautomerization

conditions.other: Shaded water; proposed pH 4-7 after mixing with mildly acidic volcanic water. Proposed transfer and trapping interval: less than 1 h. Neither the tautomer distribution nor its relaxation time is supplied by the cited research.

reactions.mechanism: Isomerization balance: PhCH=CH-SH -> PhCH2-CH=S. Proton transfer moves the double bond from C=C to C=S without changing the C8H8S formula.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE MICROSTEP RESOLUTION of the sulfur-adduct hydrolysis framework supported by Friedmann and Miller (1969). A transient thioaldehyde provides a chemically explicit route to phenylacetaldehyde, but the supplied report does not establish its accumulation or isolation. Hydrolytic trapping must compete with thioaldehyde oligomerization; the node is not an assumed stable storage pool.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic trapping of the sulfur intermediate as phenylacetaldehyde

conditions.other: Proposed pH 4-6 in shaded water, with aldehyde capture downstream within minutes to 1 h. Mild degassing removes regenerated H2S before the cyanide stage; cyanide is not yet present. Short-distance overflow into an ammoniacal receiver is the proposed transport mechanism. Transfer recovery and aldehyde lifetime must be measured.

reactions.mechanism: Net balance: C8H8S + H2O -> C8H8O + H2S. Water addition to C=S and sulfur elimination give PhCH2CHO. Across rxn_003 or rxn_004, rxn_005, and rxn_006, sulfide mediates the net hydration of phenylacetylene.
reactions.reasoning: The net sulfur-assisted conversion of phenylacetylene to phenylacetaldehyde is supported by Friedmann and Miller (1969); the partition into rxn_005 and rxn_006 is a mechanistic model. Phenylacetaldehyde instability makes prolonged storage undesirable (Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013). Degassing and rapid transfer are proposed compatibility measures, not demonstrated quantitative recovery steps.

reactions.name: Bulk-aqueous aromatic Strecker aminonitrile formation

conditions.other: Proposed pH 8-9, aldehyde 0.1-1 mM, total ammonia and cyanide each 1-10 mM, and reaction interval 1-24 h. These concentrations and times are design assumptions, not geochemically demonstrated inventories. Use shaded, partially enclosed pores to limit photolysis and gas loss. A labile Fe(II):cyanide inventory ratio below 0.01 would limit initial six-ligand cyanide sequestration to below approximately 6%; achieving that ratio in an iron-rich setting is unresolved.

reactions.mechanism: Net balance: C8H8O + NH3 + HCN -> C9H10N2 + H2O. Reversible imine or iminium formation is followed by cyanide addition at the imine carbon.
reactions.reasoning: Phenylacetaldehyde Strecker chemistry is directly supported by Friedmann and Miller (1969). Ruiz-Bermejo et al. (2013) identifies aldehyde polymerization and side reactions as important limitations of homogeneous processing. No high conversion is assigned here. Productive nitrile formation must outrun aldehyde polymerization, imine hydrolysis, HCN loss, and iron-mediated cyanide sequestration.

reactions.name: Aerosol-assisted aromatic Strecker aminonitrile formation

conditions.other: Anoxic gas-water aerosol cycling, not oxygen-bearing air. Proposed pH 8-9, aldehyde 0.1-1 mM, ammonia and cyanide each 1-10 mM, droplets 10-100 micrometers, individual droplet residence 0.1-10 s, and repeated cycling for 1-48 h. These numerical microphysical bounds are proposed tests, not reported conditions from the supplied account. Droplets return to a shaded receiver. Bound-cyanide feed variants must not inherit the reported free-cyanide yield.

reactions.mechanism: Net balance: C8H8O + NH3 + HCN -> C9H10N2 + H2O. Interfacial concentration and repeated droplet cycling support imine formation and cyanide capture while changing competition with aldehyde side chemistry.
reactions.reasoning: Ruiz-Bermejo et al. (2013) reported phenylalanine recovery up to approximately 81% from supplied phenylacetaldehyde in an aerosol-assisted system. That value applies to the reported experimental endpoint and workup, not an isolated aminonitrile yield, the atmospheric source module, or natural nitrile hydrolysis. Reproducing the chemistry under explicitly anoxic gas and environmentally attainable concentrations remains an integration requirement.

reactions.name: First-stage aminonitrile hydrolysis to phenylalaninamide

conditions.other: After aminonitrile capture, transfer into a separate shaded acidic pool. Proposed pH 1-2 and observation interval from days to months. The supplied report gives no environmental rate constant or validated residence time at these conditions. HCN and ammonia need not remain concentrated after this stage begins. Strong-acid laboratory workup must not be treated as evidence of rapid neutral-water hydrolysis.

reactions.mechanism: Net balance: C9H10N2 + H2O -> C9H12N2O. Nitrile protonation, water addition, and proton transfers produce the corresponding primary amide.
reactions.reasoning: Aminonitrile hydrolysis is part of the phenylalanine Strecker framework (Friedmann and Miller, 1969), and aerosol experiments establish recovered phenylalanine rather than universal environmental hydrolysis kinetics (Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013). Explicit amide formation is standard mechanistic chemistry, but completion within the proposed natural window is unvalidated. This is a principal bottleneck, not an assumed quantitative step.

reactions.name: Second-stage amide hydrolysis to racemic phenylalanine

conditions.temperature: 350-370 K during hydrolysis; 300-320 K after cooling
conditions.other: Proposed pH 1-2, days-to-months monitoring, followed by cooling and buffered dilution. Exact rates and recoveries are unknown from the supplied literature. Ammonia is predominantly ammonium during acid hydrolysis; the equation uses neutral parent compounds. Avoid high-temperature vent interiors and prolonged UV exposure.

reactions.mechanism: Net neutral-parent balance: C9H12N2O + H2O -> C9H11NO2 + NH3. Acid-catalyzed acyl substitution releases the amino acid and ammonia/ammonium.
reactions.reasoning: This completes the conventional Strecker hydrolysis supported by Friedmann and Miller (1969). No environmental conversion percentage is assigned because the supplied account does not resolve amide hydrolysis rates. The product should be exported from hot zones: phenylalanine undergoes substantial hydrothermal decarboxylation at much higher temperatures (Changi et al., 2012; Aspin et al., 2025). These degradation studies do not establish its exact lifetime in the proposed cooler pool.

reactions.name: Ferrous-ion capture of cyanide as ferrocyanide

conditions.other: Anoxic, initially shaded pool at proposed pH 6-8. Cyanide inventory must supply six ligands per iron; proposed total cyanide 1-10 mM and Fe(II) at or below one-sixth of that molar inventory. Monitor complexation over minutes to hours rather than assuming complete capture. Keep this reservoir separate from sulfide-rich water, which would precipitate FeS and change speciation.

reactions.mechanism: Charge- and atom-balanced equation: Fe2+ + 6 HCN -> [Fe(CN)6]4- + 6 H+. Buffering removes the released acidity without making iron a catalyst.
reactions.reasoning: Ruiz-Bermejo et al. (2013) demonstrates that iron binding initially suppresses Strecker chemistry by removing free cyanide. Ferrocyanide is therefore represented as a stoichiometric reservoir and competing sink, not a phenylalanine catalyst. Its natural inventory depends on cyanide supply, buffering, iron speciation, and competing sulfide precipitation.

reactions.name: Ferrocyanide photoaquation and conditional delivery of released HCN

conditions.other: Ruiz-Bermejo et al. reported 254 nm irradiation for 48 h; the supplied report gives no irradiance, so an experimental photon dose is not invented. Proposed environmental geometry: an illuminated 0.1-1 mm water film at pH 6-8, without aldehyde present. Partial HCN volatilization into a connected pore headspace and capture by a shaded ammoniacal receiver could separate volatile cyanide from nonvolatile iron complexes. That transport mechanism and its efficiency are hypotheses. Useful delivery requires cyanide capture to exceed rebinding, photochemical destruction, and atmospheric escape; the necessary rate constants are unavailable.

reactions.mechanism: First-ligand-release balance: [Fe(CN)6]4- + H2O + H+ -> [Fe(CN)5(H2O)]3- + HCN. This represents one photoaquation event, not instantaneous liberation of all six ligands or destruction of the iron complex.
reactions.reasoning: UV-assisted recovery of reactive cyanide and increased amino-acid formation from ferrocyanide systems are supported by Ruiz-Bermejo et al. (2013). The single aquapentacyanide product is a first-step speciation model, not a complete measured photoproduct inventory. Bound-cyanide phenylalanine recovery was much poorer than free-cyanide recovery, with competing hydroxy-acid formation. Release, rebinding, and delivery remain explicit limitations; no reservoir-fed route is assigned the approximately 81% free-cyanide yield.

reactions.name: Fresh ferrous sulfide precipitation

conditions.other: Mix anoxic ferrous water and a near-stoichiometric sulfide supply at proposed pH 8-9.5. Transfer the wet precipitate directly to the amination compartment within minutes to hours; do not dry or deliberately age it. Avoid excess dissolved sulfide and high ionic strength. These handling intervals are proposed, while the requirement for fresh material is experimentally supported.

reactions.mechanism: Net balance: Fe2+ + H2S -> FeS + 2 H+. Sulfide precipitation creates a fresh reactive Fe(II)-bearing solid; environmental alkalinity must absorb the released acidity.
reactions.reasoning: Freshly precipitated FeS, unlike aged or dried material, supported reproducible phenylpyruvate reductive amination in Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003). This preparation node is chemically necessary to specify the reactive mineral state. No particular crystalline polymorph or indefinite surface lifetime is assumed.

reactions.name: Fresh ferrous hydroxide precipitation

conditions.other: Anoxic alkaline water; proposed pH 9-10 and immediate wet transfer within minutes to hours. Carbonate and sulfide must be sufficiently low that FeCO3 or FeS does not dominate the precipitate. Alkalinity is a required boundary condition, not an unlimited reagent assumed without buffering.

reactions.mechanism: Net balance: Fe2+ + 2 H2O -> Fe(OH)2 + 2 H+. Hydroxide precipitation stores ferrous iron in a reactive reduced solid.
reactions.reasoning: Fe(OH)2 was an effective alternative to FeS for reductive amination, whereas FeCO3 was inactive in the reported comparison (Huber and Wächtershäuser, 2003). The competing precipitation constraints are therefore mechanistically important. No oxygen is used to prepare the solid.

reactions.name: Phenylpyruvate reductive amination by fresh FeS
agents: Freshly precipitated FeS: consumed Fe(II) reductant and reactive mineral surface

conditions.temperature: 348 K, corresponding to the reported 75 degrees C experiment
conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm in a closed anoxic vessel or sheltered geothermal pore
conditions.other: Reported strong-performing conditions: pH 9.2, NH4Cl nitrogen source, 17 h; a bicarbonate formulation gave similar performance at pH 9.3. Ammonia denotes the reactive fraction of the ammonium pool. Maintain fresh wet FeS, modest ionic strength, and low excess dissolved sulfide. The formal balance requires two oxidized Fe(II) equivalents per phenylalanine; actual mineral loading depends on the unknown reactive fraction.

reactions.mechanism: Formal mineral-redox balance: C9H8O3 + NH3 + 2 FeS + 3 H2O -> C9H11NO2 + 2 FeOOH + 2 H2S. An imino intermediate accepts two reducing equivalents as Fe(II) is oxidized. FeOOH is a mass- and electron-balanced ferric surface endmember, not an experimentally identified exclusive product phase; dissolved sulfide is predominantly HS- at the operating pH.
reactions.reasoning: Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003) reported phenylalanine yields up to 53 mol% with NH4Cl and 49 mol% with NH4HCO3 under the stated conditions. FeS is not treated as a turnover catalyst without regeneration. The exact oxidized solid assemblage remains a modeling uncertainty. Phenylpyruvate is supplied at the network boundary: Nakajima et al. (1975) used an activated aromatic thioester and synthetic Fe-S chemistry, while Keefe et al. (1995) cautions against assuming that CO2, FeS, and H2S alone generate the missing aromatic precursor.

reactions.name: Phenylpyruvate reductive amination by fresh Fe(OH)2
agents: Freshly precipitated Fe(OH)2: consumed Fe(II) reductant and reactive mineral surface

conditions.temperature: Approximately 348 K as a proposed matched comparison
conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm in a closed anoxic vessel or sheltered geothermal pore
conditions.other: Proposed matched comparison: pH approximately 9.2 and 17 h, with fresh wet mineral and an ammonia/ammonium pool. The supplied report establishes Fe(OH)2 activity but does not provide its exact phenylalanine optimum; the FeS optimum is not asserted to be identical. Exclude oxygen and minimize conversion of the starting solid to carbonate or sulfide.

reactions.mechanism: Formal mineral-redox balance: C9H8O3 + NH3 + 2 Fe(OH)2 -> C9H11NO2 + 2 FeOOH + H2O. Mineral-derived reducing equivalents reduce an imino intermediate. FeOOH again denotes a possible ferric oxidation-product endmember rather than a measured exclusive solid.
reactions.reasoning: Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003) directly supports Fe(OH)2-dependent reductive amination of the supplied keto-acid substrate. Barge et al. (2019) provides related mineral-redox evidence for alanine, not an independent phenylalanine synthesis. This alternative is chemically justified by its sulfur-free reducing surface, but its exact yield and mineral endpoint are not supplied. The upstream phenylpyruvate source remains unresolved.

reactions.name: Observed trace phenylalanine endpoint in a volcanic-discharge process

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk steam-mist and collection compartments; nonthermal electrical discharge
conditions.other: Anoxic, locally reduced gases contact a steam-water mist and an aqueous collector. Electrical discharge supplies energy; the active discharge channel is not constrained to the collector temperature. A 1-7 day collection interval is a proposed comparison experiment, not a duration supplied for the historical samples. Analytical recovery and any postcollection processing are part of the observation and must not be equated with immediate free-amino-acid production in the gas.

reactions.mechanism: Formal selected-product balance: 9 CH4 + NH3 + 2 H2O -> C9H11NO2 + 16 H2. This is a coarse-grained process node covering an unresolved product mixture and downstream aqueous processing, not an elementary seventeen-molecule collision or a measured overall process stoichiometry.
reactions.reasoning: Johnson et al. (2008) detected trace phenylalanine in archived volcanic-apparatus discharge material. This is the strongest supplied observational connection between simple reduced feedstocks and the target, but it does not resolve the aromatic intermediates or validate rxn_002 through rxn_010 individually. Yield and atmospheric applicability remain limited; Schlesinger and Miller (1983) supports the importance of reducing gas composition. The node is explicitly kept separate from the more detailed, only partly validated mechanism.

pathways.name: Ionic sulfur channel followed by bulk free-cyanide Strecker chemistry
pathways.description: Methane-derived source modules provide cyanide and a conditional phenylacetylene supply. Ionic sulfide addition, sulfur-intermediate hydrolysis, bulk Strecker capture, and two-stage nitrile hydrolysis lead to racemic phenylalanine. Aromatic supply, aldehyde survival, and environmental hydrolysis are unresolved bottlenecks.

pathways.name: Radical sulfur channel followed by bulk free-cyanide Strecker chemistry
pathways.description: The photoinitiated sulfur branch replaces ionic addition in P1. It is a distinct mechanistic variant, not independent evidence for an integrated synthesis. Productive irradiation must occur before aldehyde formation, and its selectivity is unquantified.

pathways.name: Ionic sulfur channel followed by aerosol free-cyanide Strecker chemistry
pathways.description: Ionic sulfur chemistry feeds a physically separate anoxic aerosol reactor. The aerosol conversion of supplied aldehyde has strong experimental support, but its reported yield is not transferred to the upstream source modules or to unvalidated natural hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Radical sulfur channel followed by aerosol free-cyanide Strecker chemistry
pathways.description: A photoinitiated sulfide-addition compartment supplies aldehyde to a shaded aerosol compartment. Spatial separation prevents assuming that an aldehyde-compatible irradiation dose exists. The integrated source-to-target pathway has not been demonstrated.

pathways.name: Ferrocyanide-buffered cyanide supply to the ionic bulk Strecker branch
pathways.description: A cyanide side branch first binds cyanide to Fe(II), then conditionally returns part of it through photoaquation. Released HCN must reach the bulk aldehyde-ammonia receiver before rebinding or escape. This is a lower-confidence supply variant and does not generate additional cyanide inventory.

pathways.name: Ferrocyanide-buffered cyanide supply to the ionic aerosol Strecker branch
pathways.description: Ionic sulfur chemistry supplies aldehyde while a separate illuminated iron-cyanide reservoir supplies only its recoverable cyanide fraction. Aerosol capture follows. The free-cyanide aerosol yield is explicitly inapplicable to this bound-cyanide route.

pathways.name: Ferrocyanide-buffered cyanide supply to the radical aerosol Strecker branch
pathways.description: Two separate irradiation modules provide the productive sulfur adduct and a recoverable cyanide fraction. Their products converge only after irradiation in the shaded aerosol receiver. This recombined variant has the largest number of unmeasured transfer and photochemical efficiencies among the listed Strecker pathways.

pathways.name: Supplied phenylpyruvate reduced on freshly precipitated FeS
pathways.description: Ferrous ion and sulfide create the experimentally important fresh mineral, which reductively aminates supplied phenylpyruvate. The terminal conversion has direct experimental support. This pathway begins at an explicitly complex precursor boundary and is not claimed to solve aromatic-carbon construction.

pathways.name: Supplied phenylpyruvate reduced on freshly precipitated Fe(OH)2
pathways.description: An alkaline, sulfide-poor compartment precipitates ferrous hydroxide, which provides reducing equivalents for phenylpyruvate amination. The mineral alternative is experimentally supported, but its exact optimum and upstream keto-acid source remain unspecified.

pathways.name: Empirical volcanic-discharge process from simple feedstocks
pathways.description: Simple reduced gases and water produce an experimentally detected trace phenylalanine endpoint after discharge, collection, and analysis. This is an observational process-level pathway with unresolved internal chemistry, not confirmation of any particular detailed aromatic mechanism.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Friedmann and Miller (1969), as summarized in the supplied research, support the sulfur-assisted phenylacetylene-to-phenylalanine route. However, rxn_002 remains an unvalidated methane-only source module, and evidence for the overall sulfur conversion does not establish every proposed intermediate separately. Bulk Strecker chemistry is credible, but aldehyde polymerization and completion of both hydrolysis stages require explicit operating conditions. The pathway is connected and conservation-consistent, but its complete implementation is not demonstrated.
suggestions: Resolve rxn_002 into experimentally supported transformations, or retain it explicitly as an unvalidated source module and measure phenylacetylene production and capture.
Specify mol_008 as PhCH=CHSH and mol_009 as PhCH2CH=S, and establish the productive regioisomer distribution and hydrolytic trapping efficiency.
Provide reaction-specific pH, temperature, concentration, residence time, and hydrolysis conditions, including competition with phenylacetaldehyde polymerization.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The radical sulfur channel is consistent with the route-family evidence summarized for Friedmann and Miller (1969). Its representation as selective formation of one thioenol nevertheless requires product-distribution evidence. The methane-to-phenylacetylene source remains unresolved, and no irradiation parameters or downstream hydrolysis conditions are supplied. A separate irradiated source compartment and aqueous reaction compartment are physically plausible; their number or ordering is not a concern.
suggestions: Measure phenylacetylene formation and recovery under a defined methane-containing discharge or photochemical protocol.
Specify radical initiation, wavelength range, photon exposure, sulfide speciation, and competing products for rxn_004.
Demonstrate transfer and aqueous trapping of the sulfur products, followed by hydrolysis to free phenylalanine under stated environmental conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ruiz-Bermejo et al. (2013) provide strong evidence for aerosol-assisted conversion of supplied phenylacetaldehyde to phenylalanine. Their reported yield supports the downstream process, not methane-to-aromatic synthesis or an isolated aminonitrile yield for rxn_008. The aerosol branch therefore strengthens target conversion without resolving rxn_002, sulfur-intermediate assignments, or the environmental implementation of rxn_009 and rxn_010.
suggestions: Map the aerosol experiment's complete preparation, cycling, collection, and hydrolysis protocol onto the corresponding network reactions.
Specify droplet residence times, reagent concentrations, and HCN/NH3 retention rather than assuming aerosolization automatically provides useful concentration.
Validate the upstream phenylacetylene source and sulfur-product structures independently of the demonstrated aerosol conversion.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This combines a literature-supported sulfur reaction family with the experimentally supported aerosol Strecker process of Ruiz-Bermejo et al. (2013). The combination is chemically coherent but has not itself been demonstrated as an integrated sequence. Radical selectivity, recovery of the productive aldehyde, and completion of hydrolysis remain insufficiently specified. The principal upstream limitation is still rxn_002, not the choice of aerosol processing.
suggestions: Quantify productive sulfur-adduct formation and aldehyde recovery under defined irradiation conditions.
Specify how aldehyde-containing water enters and is recovered from the aerosol compartment while retaining sufficient cyanide and ammonia.
Separate aminonitrile formation from subsequent hydrolysis in yield measurements, and retain the methane source step as unresolved until tested.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ferrocyanide capture and photoaquation are chemically credible, and the two parser-unchecked reactions can be balanced manually. However, Ruiz-Bermejo et al. (2013) show that iron initially sequesters cyanide and that irradiation only conditionally restores productive chemistry. The listed photoaquation releases one cyanide ligand per event; it does not establish complete ligand release or a closed recycling cycle. This delivery uncertainty compounds, rather than repairs, the unresolved aromatic source and hydrolysis conditions.
suggestions: Use the reported 254 nm, 48 h irradiation experiment as a laboratory benchmark, while separately assessing the relevant environmental spectrum and exposure.
Measure free cyanide delivery after accounting for residual bound ligands, recomplexation, volatilization, and competing chemistry.
Specify spatial or temporal management of iron and sulfide so precipitation and cyanide sequestration do not undermine the intended reservoirs.
Resolve the shared aromatic-source and hydrolysis limitations rather than treating cyanide storage as evidence for the complete pathway.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The aerosol and irradiated-ferrocyanide modules have relevant support in Ruiz-Bermejo et al. (2013), but their evidence must be distinguished: the highest reported phenylalanine yield used free cyanide, whereas metal-bound cyanide performed substantially worse. Ferrocyanide is appropriately treated as a reservoir, not a freely regenerating catalyst. Productive cyanide delivery to droplets, upstream aromatic formation, and environmentally effective hydrolysis remain unestablished.
suggestions: Report free-cyanide and ferrocyanide-fed aerosol experiments separately, including phenylalanine and competing hydroxy-acid yields.
Quantify photoreleased cyanide capture by droplets and track the cyanide remaining in aquapentacyanoferrate.
Provide compartment-specific pH, irradiation, droplet-processing, and hydrolysis conditions, with citations attached to individual reactions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The radical sulfur and ferrocyanide photochemical modules are plausible individually, but their irradiation requirements and product recoveries need separate justification. Distinct compartments can accommodate different conditions; no single shared irradiation regime is required. Literature support for aerosol Strecker chemistry does not validate selective sulfur photochemistry, efficient cyanide delivery, or the methane-only aromatic source. The pathway remains a coherent experimental proposal rather than an established complete synthesis.
suggestions: Define independent spectral exposures and residence times for sulfide addition and ferrocyanide photoaquation.
Measure survival and transfer of the productive sulfur products and released cyanide before aerosol processing.
Validate aminonitrile and amide hydrolysis under the proposed collection conditions, and distinguish module-level evidence from an integrated synthesis demonstration.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest supported pathway within its declared scope. Huber and Wachtershauser (2003) demonstrated phenylpyruvate reductive amination with fresh FeS, including approximately 53 mol% phenylalanine at pH 9.2 and 75 C for 17 h. Supplied phenylpyruvate is an allowed starting material and is not a defect. The principal qualification concerns rxn_015's specific FeOOH/H2S product representation: it is balanced redox bookkeeping, but the actual oxidized mineral assemblage is not established by the supplied evidence.
suggestions: Attach the reported pH, temperature, duration, reagent concentrations, and mineral preparation procedure directly to rxn_015.
Control oxygen exposure, excess sulfide, ionic strength, and mineral aging, all of which affect the reported reaction.
Characterize the oxidized iron and sulfur products before treating FeOOH as the actual terminal mineral phase.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Fresh Fe(OH)2-mediated reductive amination is supported by Huber and Wachtershauser (2003). The balanced consumption of two Fe(II) centers is consistent with supplying the two reducing equivalents required for the organic transformation; the mineral is not merely a passive catalyst. The route coherently produces phenylalanine from the explicitly supplied keto acid. Confidence is limited mainly by absent reaction-specific operating conditions and the unverified assignment of FeOOH as the terminal oxidation product.
suggestions: Provide the Fe(OH)2-specific experimental conditions and yields rather than automatically transferring the FeS optimum.
Document fresh precipitation, alkaline pH maintenance, anoxic handling, and mineral aging.
Identify the resulting iron phases and maintain the distinction between a formal balanced endmember and an observed reaction product.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Johnson et al. (2008), as described in the supplied research, support a trace phenylalanine endpoint in volcanic-discharge samples. Trace abundance does not itself fail the target criterion. rxn_017 is acceptable as an explicitly empirical process-level representation, but its balanced equation is not a demonstrated elementary reaction or complete product balance for the discharge mixture. Gas composition, collection conditions, and any analytical hydrolysis must be specified to determine precisely what environmental production of free phenylalanine has been demonstrated.
suggestions: Define the process boundary, including gas composition, discharge exposure, steam or mist handling, collection, and sample treatment.
Distinguish phenylalanine present before analysis from phenylalanine released from precursors during any analytical hydrolysis.
Report target abundance, blanks, and detection evidence while retaining the unresolved aromatic mechanism and complex coproduct mixture explicitly.

evaluation.network_feedback: The complete network is connected, contains sufficient molecule and reaction nodes, and uses molecule IDs consistently. Pathway reaction memberships were inferred from the supplied titles and step counts. The deterministic check reports no conservation violations. Its two unchecked reactions also balance manually: rxn_011 is Fe2+ + 6 HCN -> [Fe(CN)6]4- + 6 H+, and rxn_012 is [Fe(CN)6]4- + H2O + H+ -> [Fe(CN)5(H2O)]3- + HCN. Large coefficients in the lumped methane reactions are not themselves conservation errors, although balance does not establish a mechanism. Literature alignment is strong at the route-family level: sulfur-assisted aromatic Strecker chemistry, aerosol conversion, fresh-iron-mineral reductive amination, and a trace discharge endpoint all have relevant experimental support. The strategy appropriately acknowledges speculative aromatic sourcing, supplied phenylpyruvate, racemic product, uncertain mineral products, and conditional cyanide delivery. Nevertheless, rxn_002 remains unresolved, sulfur species are more precisely assigned than the supplied evidence establishes, and environmental completion of rxn_009 and rxn_010 is insufficiently specified. Surface or cooled geothermal compartments are plausible, but reaction-specific pH, temperature, concentrations, irradiation, residence times, and transfer efficiencies are largely absent. Reaction-level citations are also missing from the network entries.
